HR@10 with one positive and 99 sampled negatives measures success within 100 candidates; it does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly. Krichene and Rendle show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation: repeating negative sampling does not eliminate this bias. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged, but interpret gains specifically as improvements under its sampled-candidate protocol, without claiming better full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

For this benchmark, a useful paired uncertainty analysis would retain each model’s per-user hit indicator on identical users and candidates, bootstrap user pairs within each category, compute the mean hit difference per category, then average the four differences equally. Report the observed macro difference, approximate 95% bootstrap interval, and category differences. One changed hit contributes 0.5 percentage points within a 200-user category, or 0.125 percentage points to the four-category macro average. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fitted models, fixed categories and sampled candidates, assuming users are suitable independent sampling units; it excludes training-seed and negative-sampling variability. User-based statistical comparisons are discussed in [Offline evaluation options](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-020-09371-3).

Repeatedly selecting checkpoints and architectures using the same validation users creates selection optimism. A conventional paired bootstrap performed after selection does not correct that adaptive search bias; even an interval excluding zero is exploratory evidence, not independent confirmation or a guarantee about full-catalog ranking. Record search effort and checkpoint-selection rules, treat small gains cautiously, and reserve confirmation for the host’s untouched final evaluation. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
